s: gods and goddesses rain down nectar, sandal powder, flowers, gold, and pearls (at Mahâvîra's birth)
q: the gods and goddesses rained down one great shower of nectar, sandal powder, flowers, gold, and pearls.

s: gods and goddesses perform anointment as a Tîrthakara (customary ceremony)
q: the gods and goddesses (of the above-mentioned four orders) performed the customary ceremonies of auspiciousness and honour, and his anointment as a Tîrthakara.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has nurses five nurses (five kinds of nurses)
q: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was attended by five nurses: a wet-nurse, a nurse to clean him, one to dress him, one to play with him, one to carry him

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra experiences fivefold joys and pleasures (allowed and noble)
q: lived in the enjoyment of the allowed, noble, fivefold joys and pleasures

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra is a Gñâtri Kshatriya (Gñâtriputra and Videha)
q: the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, a Gñâtri Kshatriya, Gñâtriputra, a Videha

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra lives as Videha (among householders for thirty years)
q: lived thirty years amongst the householders under the name of 'Videha.'

s: Mahâvîra's renunciation of household life occurs in Uttaraphalgunî (moon in conjunction with the asterism)
q: on its tenth day, while the moon was in conjunction with Uttaraphalgunî, he made up his mind to retire from the world.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has wife Yasodâ
q: His wife Yasodâ belonged to the Kaundinya gotra.

s: Sakra creates divine pavilion (by magic)
q: There he underwent a great transformation, and produced by magic a great, beautiful, lovely, fine-shaped divine pavilion

s: Sakra creates great throne (in the middle part of the divine pavilion)
q: In the middle part of that divine pavilion he produced one great throne of the same description, with a footstool.

s: Mahâvîra's palankin Kandraprabhâ is carried by thousand men
q: the great palankin, called Kandraprabhâ, which a thousand men carry.

s: Mahâvîra's palankin Kandraprabhâ carries The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra (during his renunciation)
q: the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, in his palankin Kandraprabhâ, which only a thousand men can carry

s: Mahâvîra's renunciation of household life travels to the park Gñâtri Shanda (after leaving the northern Kshatriya part of the place Kundapura)
q: left the northern Kshatriya part of the place Kundapura by the high way for the park Gñâtri Shanda.

s: Mahâvîra's renunciation of household life includes five handfuls of hair (hair plucked from the head)
q: Mahâvîra then plucked out with his right and left (hands) on the right and left (sides of his head) his hair in five handfuls.

s: Mahâvîra's adoption of holy conduct follows Mahâvîra's renunciation of household life (after plucking out his hair)
q: After the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra had plucked out his hair in five handfuls (as described above), he paid obeisance to all liberated spirits, and vowing to do no sinful act, he adopted the holy conduct.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra possesses Manahparyâya knowledge (after adopting holy conduct)
q: he reached the knowledge called Manahparyâya

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has daughter Anoggâ
q: His daughter, who belonged to the Kâsyapa gotra, had two names: Anoggâ and Priyadarsanâ.

s: Mahâvîra's attainment of Kevala is highest knowledge and intuition (complete, full, unobstructed, unimpeded, infinite and supreme)
q: he reached Nirvâna, the complete and full, the unobstructed, unimpeded, infinite and supreme, best knowledge and intuition, called Kevala.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra attains Mahâvîra's attainment of Kevala (while in deep meditation)
q: he reached Nirvâna, the complete and full, the unobstructed, unimpeded, infinite and supreme, best knowledge and intuition, called Kevala.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra teaches law (first to gods, afterwards to men)
q: first he taught the law to the gods, afterwards to men.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra is a Arhat (after attaining Kevala)
q: When the Venerable One had become an Arhat and Gina, he was a Kevalin

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra is omniscient highest knowledge and intuition (as a Kevalin)
q: he was a Kevalin, omniscient and comprehending all objects

s: Gambûdvîpa contains Kundapura (place of Mahâvîra's conception, transfer, birth and renunciation)
q: Here, forsooth, in the continent of Gambudvîpa, in Bharatavarsha, in the southern part of it, in the southern brahmanical part of the place Kundapura

s: Uttaraphalgunî is conjoined with moon (during Mahâvîra's major life events)
q: the five (most important moments of whose life happened) when the moon was in conjunction with the asterism Uttaraphalgunî

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has granddaughter Seshavatî
q: His granddaughter, who belonged to the Kausika gotra, had two names: Seshavatî and Yasovatî.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has name Vardhamâna (given by his parents)
q: by his parents he was called Vardhamâna

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has name Sramana (because he is devoid of love and hate)
q: because he is devoid of love and hate (he is called) Sramana (i.e. Ascetic)

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has final liberation in Svâti
q: But in Svâti the Venerable One obtained final liberation.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra is a Venerable Ascetic
q: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra endowed with the highest knowledge and intuition taught the five great vows, with their clauses, the six classes of lives to the Sramanas and Nirgranthas, to Gautama, &c.

s: Nirgranthas practises the second great vow (correctly)
q: In this way the great vow is correctly practised, followed, &c. This is, Sir, the second great vow. ii.

s: Nirgranthas practises the third great vow (correctly)
q: In this way the great vow, &c. This is, Sir, the third great vow. iii.

s: Nirgranthas practises the fourth great vow (correctly)
q: In this way the great vow, &c. This is, Sir, the fourth great vow. iv.

s: Nirgranthas practises the fifth great vow (correctly)
q: In this way the great vow, &c. (see above). v.

s: Nirgranthas is careful in walking (not careless)
q: A Nirgrantha is careful in his walk, not careless.

s: Nirgranthas searches into mind (rejecting sinful, blamable, work-oriented, impulsive, divisive, quarrelsome, fault-producing, painful, injurious, or murderous minds)
q: A Nirgrantha searches into his mind (i.e. thoughts and intentions). If his mind is sinful, blamable, intent on works, acting on impulses, produces cutting and splitting (or division and dissension), quarrels, faults, and pains, injures living beings, or kills creatures, he should not employ such a mind in action; but if, on the contrary, it is not sinful, &c., then he may put it in action.

s: Nirgranthas searches into speech (not uttering sinful or harmful speech)
q: A Nirgrantha searches into his speech; if his speech is sinful, blamable, &c. (all down to) kills creatures, he should not utter that speech. But if, on the contrary, it is not sinful, &c., then he may utter it.

s: Nirgranthas is careful in laying down utensils of begging (not careless)
q: A Nirgrantha is careful in laying down his utensils of begging, he is not careless in it.

s: Nirgranthas inspects food (before eating and drinking)
q: A Nirgrantha eats and drinks after inspecting his food and drink; he does not eat and drink without inspecting his food and drink.

s: Nirgranthas speaks after deliberation (not without deliberation)
q: A Nirgrantha speaks after deliberation, not without deliberation.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has attribute the highest knowledge and intuition
q: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra endowed with the highest knowledge and intuition taught the five great vows, with their clauses, the six classes of lives to the Sramanas and Nirgranthas, to Gautama, &c.

s: Nirgranthas renounces anger (not angry)
q: A Nirgrantha comprehends (and renounces) anger, he is not angry.

s: Nirgranthas renounces greed (not greedy)
q: A Nirgrantha comprehends (and renounces) greed, he is not greedy.

s: Nirgranthas renounces fear (not afraid)
q: A Nirgrantha comprehends (and renounces) fear, he is not afraid.

s: Nirgranthas renounces mirth (not mirthful)
q: A Nirgrantha comprehends (and renounces) mirth, he is not mirthful.

s: Nirgranthas begs after deliberation (for a limited ground)
q: A Nirgrantha begs after deliberation, for a limited ground, not without deliberation.

s: Nirgranthas consumes food (with permission of the superior)
q: A Nirgrantha consumes his food and drink with permission (of his superior), not without his permission.

s: Nirgranthas takes possession of a limited part of ground (for a fixed time)
q: A Nirgrantha who has taken possession of some ground, should always take possession of a limited part of it and for a fixed time.

s: Nirgranthas renews grant (constantly)
q: A Nirgrantha who has taken possession of some ground, should constantly have his grant renewed.

s: Nirgranthas begs for a limited ground (for co-religionists, after deliberation)
q: A Nirgrantha begs for a limited ground for his co-religionists after deliberation, not without deliberation.

s: Nirgranthas renounces sexual pleasures (with gods, men, or animals)
q: I renounce all sexual pleasures, either with gods or men or animals.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra teaches the five great vows (with their clauses)
q: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra endowed with the highest knowledge and intuition taught the five great vows, with their clauses, the six classes of lives to the Sramanas and Nirgranthas, to Gautama, &c.

s: Nirgranthas does not discuss topics relating to women (continually)
q: A Nirgrantha does not continually discuss topics relating to women.

s: Nirgranthas does not contemplate lovely forms of women (does not regard or contemplate them)
q: A Nirgrantha does not regard and contemplate the lovely forms of women.

s: Nirgranthas does not recall pleasures and amusements formerly had with women (to his mind)
q: A Nirgrantha does not recall to his mind the pleasures and amusements he formerly had with women.

s: Nirgranthas does not consume excessively food (does not drink liquors or eat highly-seasoned dishes)
q: A Nirgrantha does not eat and drink too much, nor does he drink liquors or eat highly-seasoned dishes.

s: Nirgranthas does not occupy couches (affected by women, animals, or eunuchs)
q: A Nirgrantha does not occupy a bed or couch affected by women, animals, or eunuchs.

s: Nirgranthas avoids love or hate (when sounds reach the ear)
q: If it is impossible not to hear sounds, which reach the ear, the mendicant should avoid love or hate, originated by them.

s: the first great vow: abstinence from killing any living beings renounces killing living beings (whether subtile or gross, movable or immovable)
q: I renounce all killing of living beings, whether subtile or gross, whether movable or immovable.

s: the second great vow renounces lying speech (arising from anger, greed, fear, or mirth)
q: I renounce all vices of lying speech (arising) from anger or greed or fear or mirth.

s: the third great vow renounces taking anything not given (in a village, town, or wood; living or lifeless; little or much; small or great)
q: I renounce all taking of anything not given, either in a village or a town or a wood, either of little or much, of small or great, of living or lifeless things.

s: the fourth great vow renounces sexual pleasures (with gods, men, or animals)
q: I renounce all sexual pleasures, either with gods or men or animals.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra teaches the six classes of lives (to the Sramanas and Nirgranthas and to Gautama)
q: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra endowed with the highest knowledge and intuition taught the five great vows, with their clauses, the six classes of lives to the Sramanas and Nirgranthas, to Gautama, &c.

s: the fifth great vow renounces attachments (whether little or much, small or great, living or lifeless)
q: I renounce all attachments, whether little or much, small or great, living or lifeless; neither shall I myself form such attachments, nor cause others to do so, nor consent to their doing so, &c. (all down to) exempt myself.

s: the fifth great vow has clause sounds (the first clause concerns agreeable and disagreeable sounds)
q: If a creature with ears hears agreeable and disagreeable sounds, it should not be attached to, nor delighted with, nor desiring of, nor infatuated by, nor covetous of, nor disturbed by the agreeable or disagreeable sounds.

s: the fifth great vow has clause forms (the second clause concerns agreeable and disagreeable forms)
q: If a creature with eyes sees agreeable and disagreeable forms (or colours), it should not be attached, &c., to them.

s: the fifth great vow has clause smells (the third clause concerns agreeable and disagreeable smells)
q: If a creature with an organ of smell smells agreeable or disagreeable smells, it should not be attached to them.

s: the fifth great vow has clause tastes (the fourth clause concerns agreeable and disagreeable tastes)
q: If a creature with a tongue tastes agreeable or disagreeable tastes, it should not be attached, &c., to them.

s: the fifth great vow has clause touches (the fifth clause concerns agreeable and disagreeable touches)
q: If a creature with an organ of feeling feels agreeable or disagreeable touches, it should not be attached to them.

s: the five great vows has part twenty-five clauses
q: He who is well provided with these great vows and their twenty-five clauses is really Houseless, if he, according to the sacred lore, the precepts, and the way correctly practises, follows, executes, explains, establishes, and, according to the precept, effects them.

s: the six classes of lives has part animals (one of six classes)
q: The six classes of lives are earth-body, &c. (down to) animals. (29)

s: Nirgranthas is a Houseless (when well provided with the great vows and their twenty-five clauses)
q: He who is well provided with these great vows and their twenty-five clauses is really Houseless, if he, according to the sacred lore, the precepts, and the way correctly practises, follows, executes, explains, establishes, and, according to the precept, effects them.

s: Nirgranthas practises the first great vow: abstinence from killing any living beings (correctly, according to the precept)
q: In this way the great vow is correctly practised, followed, executed, explained, established, effected according to the precept. This is, Sir, the first great vow: Abstinence from killing any living beings. i.

s: Sixteenth Lecture, Called the Liberation is a lecture
q: Sixteenth Lecture, Called the Liberation.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) collects alms
q: the matchless sage, who collects his alms

s: mendicant (the wise sage) frees himself from family bonds (fearlessly)
q: The wise man should free himself from the family bonds; fearless should he give up acts and attachments.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) gives up acts and attachments (fearlessly)
q: fearless should he give up acts and attachments.

s: people insult mendicant (the wise sage) (with words and blows)
q: A mendicant, living thus, self-controlled towards the eternal (world of living beings), the matchless sage, who collects his alms, is insulted with words by the people assailing him, like an elephant in battle with arrows.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) sustains words and blows (with undisturbed mind)
q: Despised by such-like people, the wise man, with undisturbed mind, sustains their words and blows, as a rock is not shaken by the wind.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) lives with monks (clever and insensible to pain and pleasure)
q: Disregarding (all calamities) he lives together with clever (monks, insensible) to pain and pleasure

s: mendicant (the wise sage) does not hurt movable and immovable beings
q: not hurting the movable and immovable (beings), not killing, bearing all

s: mendicant (the wise sage) is a good Sramana (great sage)
q: so is described the great sage, a good Sramana.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) increases austerity (while steadfast and suffering pain)
q: As the lustre of a burning flame increases, so increase the austerity, wisdom, and glory of a steadfast sage who, with vanquished desires, meditates on the supreme place of virtue, though suffering pain.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) increases wisdom (while steadfast and suffering pain)
q: so increase the austerity, wisdom, and glory of a steadfast sage who, with vanquished desires, meditates on the supreme place of virtue, though suffering pain.

s: Sixteenth Lecture, Called the Liberation is called the Liberation
q: Sixteenth Lecture, Called the Liberation.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) increases glory (while steadfast and suffering pain)
q: so increase the austerity, wisdom, and glory of a steadfast sage who, with vanquished desires, meditates on the supreme place of virtue, though suffering pain.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) meditates on supreme place of virtue (with vanquished desires)
q: who, with vanquished desires, meditates on the supreme place of virtue

s: the five great vows are a place of peace (and producers of disinterestedness)
q: The great vows which are called the place of peace, the great teachers, and the producers of disinterestedness

s: the five great vows are proclaimed by Gina (in all quarters of the earth)
q: have, in all quarters of the earth, been proclaimed by the infinite Gina

s: Gina is a knowing one (infinite)
q: the infinite Gina, the knowing one

s: Gina illumines three worlds (as light)
q: as light, illumining the three worlds, (repels) darkness.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) leads life of a mendicant (while living amongst householders)
q: The unbound one, living amongst the bound (i.e. householders), should lead the life of a mendicant

s: mendicant (the wise sage) is unattached to women
q: unattached to women, he should speak with reverence.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) does not desire this or the next world (as a learned one)
q: Not desiring this or the next world, the learned one is not measured by the qualities of love.

s: Sixteenth Lecture, Called the Liberation ends Second Book
q: End of the Sixteenth Lecture, called the Liberation. End of the Second Book.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) walks in wisdom and restraint (constant and bearing pain)
q: a thus liberated mendicant who walks in wisdom (and restraint), who is constant, and bears pain

s: mendicant (the wise sage) walks free from desire (with conquered sensuality)
q: He lives, forsooth, in accordance with wisdom (and restraint), and walks free from desire, and with conquered sensuality.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) has conquered sensuality
q: and walks free from desire, and with conquered sensuality.

s: samsâra is a boundless flood of water (difficult to traverse with the arms alone)
q: As they call the great ocean a boundless flood of water, difficult to traverse with the arms (alone), so should the learned one know (and renounce) it (the samsâra)

s: Maker of the end is a sage (one who knows and renounces samsâra)
q: so should the learned one know (and renounce) it (the samsâra): that sage is called 'Maker of the end.'

s: Maker of the end knows bondage and deliverance (according to the doctrine of the church)
q: he who, according to that doctrine (of the church), knows bondage and deliverance: that sage is called 'Maker of the end.'

s: bondage and deliverance are declared amongst men
q: Here amongst men bondage and deliverance have been declared

s: path of births is quitted by he (for whom there is no bondage whatever in this world, and besides in the two other continents, or heaven and hell)
q: He for whom there is no bondage whatever in this world, and besides in the two (other continents, or heaven and hell), is indeed a (monk needing) no support and no standing place; he has quitted the path of births.

s: Maker of the end has quitted path of births (having no bondage whatever)
q: He for whom there is no bondage whatever in this world, and besides in the two (other continents, or heaven and hell), is indeed a (monk needing) no support and no standing place; he has quitted the path of births.

s: Second Book ends Âkârâṅga Sûtra
q: End of the Second Book. End of the Âkârâṅga Sûtra.

s: Maker of the end has no support (as a monk)
q: is indeed a (monk needing) no support and no standing place

s: Maker of the end has no standing place (as a monk)
q: is indeed a (monk needing) no support and no standing place

s: Âkârâṅga Sûtra ends Second Book (after the Sixteenth Lecture)
q: End of the Sixteenth Lecture, called the Liberation. End of the Second Book. End of the Âkârâṅga Sûtra.

s: living beings attain temporary residence (in one of the four states of being)
q: The creatures attain only a temporary residence (in one of the four states of being); hearing this supreme truth (i.e. the doctrine of the Tîrthakara's) one should meditate upon it.

s: supreme truth is a doctrine (of the Tîrthakara)
q: hearing this supreme truth (i.e. the doctrine of the Tîrthakara's) one should meditate upon it.

s: Tîrthakara has doctrine supreme truth
q: hearing this supreme truth (i.e. the doctrine of the Tîrthakara's) one should meditate upon it.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) is a sage (matchless and great)
q: A mendicant, living thus, self-controlled towards the eternal (world of living beings), the matchless sage, who collects his alms, is insulted with words by the people assailing him, like an elephant in battle with arrows.

s: mendicant (the wise sage) is self controlled self-controlled (towards the eternal world of living beings)
q: A mendicant, living thus, self-controlled towards the eternal (world of living beings)

s: Third Lesson is a lesson
q: Third Lesson.

s: nuns hasten to there (on hearing or being told of some festivity)
q: A monk or a nun, hearing or being told of some festivity, might hasten there, rejoicing inwardly: 'There will be an entertainment, sure enough!'

s: Sramanas should obtain alms (from other families and eat their meal)
q: But they should enter there, and getting from other families their alms, should eat their meal.

s: nuns should obtain alms (from other families and eat their meal)
q: But they should enter there, and getting from other families their alms, should eat their meal.

s: Sramanas should not resolve to go to village (for the sake of an entertainment)
q: A monk or a nun, knowing that in a village or a scot-free town, &c. (see I, 7, 6, § 4), an entertainment will be given, should not resolve to go to that village, &c., for the sake of the entertainment.

s: nuns should not resolve to go to village (for the sake of an entertainment)
q: A monk or a nun, knowing that in a village or a scot-free town, &c. (see I, 7, 6, § 4), an entertainment will be given, should not resolve to go to that village, &c., for the sake of the entertainment.

s: much-frequented and vulgar entertainment causes injury (through crowding and unacceptable exchanges)
q: When a man goes to a much-frequented and vulgar entertainment somebody's foot treads on his foot, somebody's hand moves his hand, somebody's bowl clashes against his bowl, somebody's head comes in collision with his head, somebody's body pushes his body, or somebody beats him with a stick or a bone or a fist or a clod, or sprinkles him with cold water, or covers him with dust; or he eats unacceptable food, or he receives what should be given to others.

s: Nirgrantha should not resolve to go to much-frequented and vulgar entertainment (to partake of it)
q: Therefore should a well-controlled Nirgrantha not resolve to go to a much-frequented and vulgar entertainment to partake of it.

s: Sramanas should not accept food (on a begging-tour when its acceptability is doubtful)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept such food, &c,, about the acceptability or unacceptability of which his (or her) mind has some doubts or misgivings for such food, &c.

s: nuns should not accept food (on a begging-tour when its acceptability is doubtful)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept such food, &c,, about the acceptability or unacceptability of which his (or her) mind has some doubts or misgivings for such food, &c.

s: begging-tour involves food (whose acceptability must be certain)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept such food, &c,, about the acceptability or unacceptability of which his (or her) mind has some doubts or misgivings for such food, &c.

s: Kevalin says this is the reason
q: The Kevalin says this is the reason:

s: Sramanas should enter with complete outfit (when entering a householder's abode)
q: When a monk or a nun wishes to enter the abode of a householder, they should do so with the complete outfit.

s: nuns should enter with complete outfit (when entering a householder's abode)
q: When a monk or a nun wishes to enter the abode of a householder, they should do so with the complete outfit.

s: Sramanas should enter or leave with complete outfit (in out-of-door places for religious practices or study)
q: A monk or a nun entering or leaving the out-of-door places for religious practices or study, should do so with the complete outfit.

s: nuns should enter or leave with complete outfit (in out-of-door places for religious practices or study)
q: A monk or a nun entering or leaving the out-of-door places for religious practices or study, should do so with the complete outfit.

s: Sramanas should wander with complete outfit (when wandering from village to village)
q: A monk or a nun wandering from village to village should do so with the complete outfit.

s: nuns should wander with complete outfit (when wandering from village to village)
q: A monk or a nun wandering from village to village should do so with the complete outfit.

s: Sramanas should not enter or leave with complete outfit (when strong rain, mist, dust-raising wind, or many flying insects are present)
q: A monk or a nun should not, with the complete outfit, enter or leave the abode of a householder to collect alms, or the out-of-door places for religious practices and study, or wander from village to village on perceiving that a strong and widely-spread rain pours down, or a strong and widely-spread mist is coming on, or a high wind raises much dust, or many flying insects are scattered about and fall down.

s: nuns should not enter or leave with complete outfit (when strong rain, mist, dust-raising wind, or many flying insects are present)
q: A monk or a nun should not, with the complete outfit, enter or leave the abode of a householder to collect alms, or the out-of-door places for religious practices and study, or wander from village to village on perceiving that a strong and widely-spread rain pours down, or a strong and widely-spread mist is coming on, or a high wind raises much dust, or many flying insects are scattered about and fall down.

s: food is impure and unacceptable when obtained from Kshatriyas, kings, messengers, or relations of kings (inside or outside their houses)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept food, &c., in the houses of Kshatriyas, kings, messengers, and relations of kings, whether they are inside or outside, or invite them; for such food, &c., is impure and unacceptable.

s: alms are unacceptable when obtained from Kshatriyas, kings, messengers, or relations of kings (on a begging-tour)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept food, &c., in the houses of Kshatriyas, kings, messengers, and relations of kings, whether they are inside or outside, or invite them; for such food, &c., is impure and unacceptable.

s: Nirgrantha is a Nirgrantha (well-controlled)
q: Therefore should a well-controlled Nirgrantha not resolve to go to any festival which is preceded or followed by a feast.

s: festive entertainment is preceded or followed by feast
q: any festival which is preceded or followed by a feast

s: Nirgrantha should not resolve to go to festive entertainment (when preceded or followed by a feast)
q: Therefore should a well-controlled Nirgrantha not resolve to go to any festival which is preceded or followed by a feast.

s: sin multiplies continuously
q: These are the causes to sin, they multiply continuously.

s: Sramanas should not hasten to festive entertainment (on hearing or being told of it)
q: A monk or a nun, hearing or being told of some festivity, might hasten there, rejoicing inwardly: 'There will be an entertainment, sure enough!'

s: begging-tour does not go to funeral dinner
q: nor to a funeral dinner or to a family dinner where something is served up

s: begging-tour does not go to a family dinner where something is served up
q: nor to a funeral dinner or to a family dinner where something is served up

s: nun is a monk (as a member of the class)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour

s: crowded assembly contains Sramanas (many have arrived or will arrive)
q: or if there have arrived or will arrive many Sramanas and Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars, and if it will be a crowded assembly

s: crowded assembly contains beggars (many have arrived or will arrive)
q: or if there have arrived or will arrive many Sramanas and Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars, and if it will be a crowded assembly

s: monk may attend festive entertainment (when the route has few living beings, seeds, and related obstacles and the gathering is not crowded)
q: A monk or a nun may go to such an entertainment (as described in the preceding Sara), provided that on their way there, there are few living beings, few seeds, &c.; that no Sramanas and Brâhmanas, &c., have arrived or will arrive; that it is not a crowded assembly

s: nun may attend festive entertainment (when the route has few living beings, seeds, and related obstacles and the gathering is not crowded)
q: A monk or a nun may go to such an entertainment (as described in the preceding Sara), provided that on their way there, there are few living beings, few seeds, &c.; that no Sramanas and Brâhmanas, &c., have arrived or will arrive; that it is not a crowded assembly

s: monk undertakes begging-tour (as a mendicant)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour

s: householder has householder's abode (as the residence entered for alms)
q: A monk or a nun desirous to enter the abode of a householder

s: householder's abode contains milch cows (when they are being milked)
q: when they see that the milch cows are being milked, or the food, &c., is being cooked, and that it is not yet distributed

s: householder's abode contains food (being cooked and not yet distributed)
q: or the food, &c., is being cooked, and that it is not yet distributed

s: monk may enter the householder's abode (for the sake of alms)
q: then they may circumspectly enter or leave the householder's abode for the sake of alms

s: nun enters householder's abode (for the sake of alms after food is prepared and distributed)
q: then they may circumspectly enter or leave the householder's abode for the sake of alms

s: monk follow same rules of conduct (as a shared discipline)
q: Some of the mendicants say to those who follow the same rules of conduct, live (in the same place), or wander from village to village

s: monk live in the same place
q: Some of the mendicants say to those who follow the same rules of conduct, live (in the same place), or wander from village to village

s: village is small (described as too populous and not large)
q: This is indeed a small village, it is too populous, nor is it large

s: monk beg outlying villages (when directed away from a small, populous village)
q: reverend gentlemen, go to the outlying villages to beg alms

s: monk have kinsmen or relations (in some families)
q: Some mendicant may have there kinsmen or relations

s: nun undertakes begging-tour (as a mendicant)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour

s: kinsmen or relations include householder (examples of family connection)
q: e. g. a householder or his wife, or daughters, or daughters-in-law, or nurses, or male and female slaves or servants

s: monk accept alms (at the proper time from families connected by kindred or marriage)
q: But, at the proper time, entering there with the other mendicants, he may there in these or other families accept alms which are acceptable and given out of respect for his cloth, and eat his meal

s: alms is given for clothes (out of respect)
q: accept alms which are acceptable and given out of respect for his cloth

s: monk possess alms-bowl (used after eating and drinking)
q: after having eaten and drunk, and having cleaned and rubbed the alms-bowl

s: monk eat feast (after accepting alms at the proper time)
q: he may there in these or other families accept alms which are acceptable and given out of respect for his cloth, and eat his meal

s: begging-tour does not go to a festival (preceded or followed by an entertainment)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not resolve to go to a festival, preceded or followed by an entertainment, to partake of it

s: festive entertainment serves meat or fish (chiefly)
q: when they know that there will be served up chiefly meat or fish or roasted slices of meat or fish

s: festive entertainment serves roasted slices of meat or fish (chiefly)
q: when they know that there will be served up chiefly meat or fish or roasted slices of meat or fish

s: begging-tour does not go to wedding breakfast (in the husband's house or in that of the bride's father)
q: nor to a wedding breakfast in the husband's house or in that of the bride's father

s: Nirgrantha takes part in begging-tour (while seeking alms)
q: When a monk or a nun on a begging-tour comes upon walls or gates, or bolts or holes to fit them, they should, in case there be a byway, avoid those (obstacles), and not go on straight.

s: Nirgrantha uses heap of ashes or bones (after repeatedly examining and cleaning it)
q: on a heap of ashes or bones, &c. (see II, 1, 1, § 2), which he has repeatedly examined and cleaned, he should circumspectly wipe or rub, warm or dry (his body).

s: Nirgrantha avoids vicious animal or person (when a byway exists)
q: When a monk or a nun on a begging-tour perceives a vicious cow coming towards them, or a vicious buffalo coming towards them, or a vicious man, horse, elephant, lion, tiger, wolf, panther, bear, hyena, sarabha, shakal, cat, dog, boar, fox, leopard coming towards them, they should, in case there be a byway, circumspectly avoid them, and not walk on straight.

s: Nirgrantha requires permission for entrance of a householder's abode (before making it passable or entering or leaving)
q: they should not, without having previously got the (owner's) permission, and having examined and swept (the entrance), make it passable or enter and leave (the house).

s: Nirgrantha stays apart where no people pass or see him
q: Knowing this, he should go apart and stay where no people pass or see him.

s: Nirgrantha does not stand opposite householder's abode (when another mendicant has already entered)
q: they should not stand in their sight or opposite the door.

s: Kevalin says This is the reason
q: The Kevalin says: This is the reason:

s: food is given for Sramanas (for the sake of all of them)
q: this food, &c., has been given for the sake of all of you; eat it or divide it among you.

s: food is given for beggars (for the sake of all of them)
q: this food, &c., is given for the sake of all of you; eat it or divide it among you.

s: division of food excludes portion of food (a disproportionately large personal share)
q: Dividing the food, &c., he should not (select) for himself too great a portion

s: Nirgrantha avoids obstacle (when a byway exists)
q: When a monk or a nun on a begging-tour comes upon walls or gates, or bolts or holes to fit them, they should, in case there be a byway, avoid those (obstacles), and not go on straight.

s: division of food excludes vegetables (as a personally preferred share)
q: or the vegetables, or the conspicuous things, or the savoury things, or the delicious things, or the nice things, or the big things

s: division of food excludes conspicuous things (as a personally preferred share)
q: or the vegetables, or the conspicuous things, or the savoury things, or the delicious things, or the nice things, or the big things

s: division of food is impartial equal distribution (without eagerness, desire, greed, or covetousness)
q: but he should impartially divide it, not being eager or desirous or greedy or covetous (of anything).

s: sinful conduct is sinful
q: As this would be sinful, he should not do so.

s: Nirgrantha shares food (with other beggars)
q: Knowing this, he should join the other beggars, and after consideration say unto them: 'O long-lived Sramanas! this food, &c., is given for the sake of all of you; eat it or divide it among you.'

s: Nirgrantha practices whole duty (as stated in the lesson)
q: This certainly is the whole duty, &c.

s: Nirgrantha has body contamination (after stumbling or falling)
q: when he stumbles or falls down, his body might become contaminated with fæces, urine, phlegmatic humour, mucus, saliva, bile, matter, semen, or blood.

s: Nirgrantha does not clean body contamination (on living or unsuitable surfaces)
q: if his body has become soiled, he should not wipe or rub or scratch or clean or warm or dry it on the bare ground or wet earth [or dusty earth] on a rock or a piece of clay containing life, or timber inhabited by worms, or anything containing eggs, living beings, &c. (down to) cobwebs

s: Nirgrantha begs for straw or leaves (to clean or dry the body)
q: but he should first beg for some straw or leaves, wood or a potsherd, which must be free from dust

s: Nirgrantha begs for wood or a potsherd (to clean or dry the body)
q: but he should first beg for some straw or leaves, wood or a potsherd, which must be free from dust

s: Nirgrantha uses secluded spot (for cleaning or drying the body)
q: resort with it to a secluded spot

q: Sixth Lesson.

q: the householder's abode

q: the door-post of the householder's abode

s: householder's abode has part spitting-pot
q: his sink or spitting-pot

q: in sight of, or opposite to his bathroom or privy

s: householder's abode has part privy
q: in sight of, or opposite to his bathroom or privy

q: a loophole or a mended spot or a fissure (of the house)

s: householder's abode has part mended spot
q: a loophole or a mended spot or a fissure (of the house)

s: householder's abode has part fissure
q: a loophole or a mended spot or a fissure (of the house)

s: householder's abode has part bathing-house
q: or the bathing-house

s: food is impure impure (when given from a hand, pot, spoon, or plate treated with cold or hot water)
q: But he should not accept anything out of such a hand, &c., which has been before treated thus; for it is impure and unacceptable.

s: food is unacceptable unacceptable (when given from a hand, pot, spoon, or plate treated with cold or hot water)
q: But he should not accept anything out of such a hand, &c., which has been before treated thus; for it is impure and unacceptable.

q: for such food, &c., is pure and acceptable.

s: food is acceptable acceptable (when given with a similarly soiled hand to one similarly soiled or unsoiled)
q: for such food, &c., is pure and acceptable.

s: flattened grains is unacceptable unacceptable (when ground or winnowed for the mendicant on living material)
q: for such large, parched grains, &c., are impure and unacceptable.

s: nun is a mendicant
q: When a monk or a nun on a begging-tour perceives that many hungry animals have met and come together in search of food

s: food is prepared over fire
q: food, &c., which is prepared over the fire

s: fire has part fire-bodies
q: A layman will kill the fire-bodies

s: Kevalin states reason (for rejecting food prepared over fire)
q: The Kevalin says: This is the reason: A layman will kill the fire-bodies

s: monk uses begging-tour (while begging)
q: When a monk or a nun on a begging-tour perceives that many hungry animals have met and come together in search of food

s: nun uses begging-tour (while begging)
q: When a monk or a nun on a begging-tour perceives that many hungry animals have met and come together in search of food

s: hungry animals search for food (in groups)
q: many hungry animals have met and come together in search of food

s: householder may use handmill (to fetch food for the mendicant)
q: The layman might fetch and erect a stool or a bench or a ladder or a handmill, get upon it, and getting upon it fall or tumble down.

s: householder may cause injury (by falling or tumbling down)
q: Thus he might hurt his foot or arm or breast or belly or head or some other part of his body;

s: injury affects living beings (through killing, frightening, bruising, smashing, crushing, afflicting, paining or dislocating)
q: or he might kill or frighten or bruise or smash or crush or afflict or pain or dislocate all sorts of living beings.

s: Nirgrantha should not accept food (taken from a granary or vault by contorting the layman up and down and horizontally)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept food, &c., which a layman, for the sake of the mendicant, has taken from a granary or vault by contorting himself up and down and horizontally;

s: food is kept in earthenware vessel
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept food, &c., which is kept in earthenware.

s: householder may injure earth-body (by breaking the earthen vessel containing the food)
q: The layman might, for the sake of the mendicant, break the earthen vessel containing the food, &c., and thereby injure the earth-body;

s: householder may injure fire-body (by breaking the earthen vessel containing the food)
q: in the same way he might injure the fire-body, the wind-body, plants and animals;

s: householder may injure wind-body (by breaking the earthen vessel containing the food)
q: in the same way he might injure the fire-body, the wind-body, plants and animals;

s: pakkhâkamma sin is committed by householder (by putting the food again in earthenware)
q: by putting it again (in earthenware), he commits the pakkhâkamma sin.

s: Nirgrantha participates in begging-tour (while on the tour)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept food, &c., which has been placed on a post or pillar or beam or scaffold or loft or platform or roof or some such-like elevated place;

s: food is placed on vegetable or animal matter (and is therefore impure and unacceptable)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept food, &c., which is placed on vegetable or animal matter; for such food is impure and unacceptable.

s: water is taken from ground (and is not acceptable)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept such water as has been taken from the bare ground, &c.

s: water is associated with cobwebs (as water that should not be accepted)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept such water as has been taken from the bare ground, &c. (see II, 1, 5, § 2, all down to) cobwebs

s: food is impure impure (when fetched from above)
q: for such food fetched from above is impure and unacceptable.

s: food is unacceptable unacceptable (when fetched from above)
q: for such food fetched from above is impure and unacceptable.

s: householder may use stool (to fetch food for the mendicant)
q: The layman might fetch and erect a stool or a bench or a ladder or a handmill, get upon it, and getting upon it fall or tumble down.

q: The layman might fetch and erect a stool or a bench or a ladder or a handmill, get upon it, and getting upon it fall or tumble down.

s: Eighth Lesson is a lesson
q: Eighth Lesson.

s: monk should not accept raw powdered fruits (when not well ground and still containing small seeds)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept raw, powdered fruits which are not well ground and still contain small seeds, as those of Umbara, Pilamkhu, Nyagrodha, and Asvattha; for &c.

s: monk should not accept unripe wild rice (when old or containing, engendering, growing, or thriving living beings, or when such beings are not taken out, killed, or destroyed)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept unripe wild rice, dregs, honey, liquor, ghee, or sediments of liquor, if these things be old or if living beings are engendered or grow or thrive in them, or are not taken out, or killed or destroyed in them.

s: monk should not accept dregs (when old or containing, engendering, growing, or thriving living beings, or when such beings are not taken out, killed, or destroyed)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept unripe wild rice, dregs, honey, liquor, ghee, or sediments of liquor, if these things be old or if living beings are engendered or grow or thrive in them, or are not taken out, or killed or destroyed in them.

s: monk should not accept honey (when old or containing, engendering, growing, or thriving living beings, or when such beings are not taken out, killed, or destroyed)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept unripe wild rice, dregs, honey, liquor, ghee, or sediments of liquor, if these things be old or if living beings are engendered or grow or thrive in them, or are not taken out, or killed or destroyed in them.

s: monk should not accept ghee (when old or containing, engendering, growing, or thriving living beings, or when such beings are not taken out, killed, or destroyed)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept unripe wild rice, dregs, honey, liquor, ghee, or sediments of liquor, if these things be old or if living beings are engendered or grow or thrive in them, or are not taken out, or killed or destroyed in them.

s: monk should not accept sediments of liquor (when old or containing, engendering, growing, or thriving living beings, or when such beings are not taken out, killed, or destroyed)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept unripe wild rice, dregs, honey, liquor, ghee, or sediments of liquor, if these things be old or if living beings are engendered or grow or thrive in them, or are not taken out, or killed or destroyed in them.

s: living beings are present in liquor (when engendered, growing, or thriving in it)
q: if living beings are engendered or grow or thrive in them

s: monk should not accept raw plants (such as Ikshumeru, Aṅkakarelu, Kaseru, Samghâtika, and Pûtiâlu)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept any such-like raw plants as Ikshumeru, Aṅkakarelu, Kaseru, Samghâtika, Pûtiâlu.

s: monk should not accept Nymphaea (as a raw vegetable or plant part)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept any such-like (vegetables) as Nymphaea or stalk of Nymphaea or the bulb of Nelumbium or the upper part or the filament of Lotus or any part of the plant.

s: monk participates in begging-tour
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept juice of mangos, inspissated juice of mangos, juice of wood-apples, citrons, grapes, wild dates, pomegranates, cocoa-nuts, bamboos, jujubes, myrobalans, tamarinds, or any such-like liquor containing particles of the shell or skin or seeds, which liquor the layman, for the sake of the mendicant, pressed, strained, or filtered through a basket, cloth, or a cow's tail; for such liquor is impure and unacceptable.

s: monk should not accept Nelumbium (as the bulb)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept any such-like (vegetables) as Nymphaea or stalk of Nymphaea or the bulb of Nelumbium or the upper part or the filament of Lotus or any part of the plant.

s: monk should not accept Lotus (as its upper part or filament or any part of the plant)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept any such-like (vegetables) as Nymphaea or stalk of Nymphaea or the bulb of Nelumbium or the upper part or the filament of Lotus or any part of the plant.

s: monk should not accept raw substances (when seeds or sprouts grow on the top, root, stem, or knots of a plant)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept such-like raw substances as seeds or sprouts, growing on the top or the root or the stem or the knots (of a plant), likewise the pulp or blossoms of the plantain, cocoa-nut, wild date, and palmyra trees.

s: monk should not accept sugar-cane (when full of holes, withering, peeling off, or corroded by wolves)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept any such-like raw unmodified substances as sugar-cane, which is full of holes, or withering or peeling off or corroded by wolves

s: monk should not accept garlic (including its leaves, stalk, bulb, or integument)
q: The same holds good with regard to garlic or its leaves or stalk or bulb or integument.

s: monk should not accept Atthiya (when cooked)
q: Likewise with regard to cooked fruits of Atthiya, Tinduka, Vilva, Srîparnî.

s: monk should not accept liquor (when containing particles of shell, skin, or seeds and processed for the mendicant)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept juice of mangos, inspissated juice of mangos, juice of wood-apples, citrons, grapes, wild dates, pomegranates, cocoa-nuts, bamboos, jujubes, myrobalans, tamarinds, or any such-like liquor containing particles of the shell or skin or seeds, which liquor the layman, for the sake of the mendicant, pressed, strained, or filtered through a basket, cloth, or a cow's tail; for such liquor is impure and unacceptable.

s: monk should not accept Tinduka (when cooked)
q: Likewise with regard to cooked fruits of Atthiya, Tinduka, Vilva, Srîparnî.

s: monk should not accept Vilva (when cooked)
q: Likewise with regard to cooked fruits of Atthiya, Tinduka, Vilva, Srîparnî.

s: monk should not accept Srîparnî (when cooked)
q: Likewise with regard to cooked fruits of Atthiya, Tinduka, Vilva, Srîparnî.

s: monk should not accept corn (as raw, unmodified substances)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept such raw, unmodified substances as corn, clumps of corn, cakes of corn, sesamum, ground sesamum, or cakes of sesamum.

s: monk should not accept sesamum (as raw, unmodified substances)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept such raw, unmodified substances as corn, clumps of corn, cakes of corn, sesamum, ground sesamum, or cakes of sesamum.

s: whole duty is stated as complete
q: This is the whole duty, &c.

s: liquor is impure impure
q: for such liquor is impure and unacceptable.
